paragraphs.heading: Reactions as collisions
paragraphs.text: Collision theory is a principle chemists use to predict how fast reactions go. It says reacting particles must strike each other with the right orientation, and even then only some of these hits produce a noticeable change; those are called successful collisions. A successful collision also needs enough energy at the moment of impact, called the activation energy, to break the existing bonds and form all the new ones. That is how the products of the reaction come about.

paragraphs.heading: Origins
paragraphs.text: Max Trautz proposed collision theory in 1916, and William Lewis came up with it independently in 1918. It was first developed for gas reactions with no dilution. Most reactions, though, take place in solutions, from gas reactions carried in an inert gas to almost all reactions in solution. There, how often the dissolved molecules collide is controlled by diffusion, or Brownian motion, of single molecules.

paragraphs.heading: More hits, faster reactions
paragraphs.text: Raising the concentration of a reactant gives more collisions, and so more successful ones. Heating things up gives the molecules more kinetic energy on average, so more of their collisions carry enough energy. When a catalyst takes part in the collision, the change needs less energy, so more collisions have enough. In each case the reaction rate goes up.

paragraphs.heading: Picturing a collision
paragraphs.text: In the theory, two particles A and B collide if their nuclei come closer than a certain distance. The area around A in which an incoming B can hit it is called the cross section, σ_AB. In simple terms it is a circle whose radius is the two molecules' radii added together, treating both as spheres. This is the classical picture of solid balls; real molecules are quantum-mechanical systems, so a more general definition bases the cross section on the probability of reaction instead.

paragraphs.heading: Explaining Arrhenius
paragraphs.text: The rate expression that collision theory produces is similar to the Arrhenius equation. It gave the first theoretical explanation of that equation in terms of molecules. Its product zρ matches the pre-exponential factor of the Arrhenius equation. The theory predicts that this factor depends weakly on temperature, but the effect is so small next to the exponential part that it cannot be measured.

paragraphs.heading: Where it falls short
paragraphs.text: When its predicted rate constants are compared with known ones, collision theory gets them wrong, and it does worse the more complex the molecules are. The reason is that it assumes particles are spheres that can react from any direction, but a collision's orientation is not always right for reacting. In the hydrogenation of ethylene, for example, the H₂ molecule must come in toward the region where the atoms are bonded, and few collisions manage it. Usually the more complex the reacting molecules, the lower the steric factor. Harpoon reactions, in which atoms exchange electrons and form ions, are an exception, with steric factors greater than one.
